subject: language_arts

unit.title: Word classes & sentence types
unit.essentialQuestion: What jobs do words do, and how do sentences come in different types?

title: Expanded noun phrases (paint a picture)
objectives: By the end, I can expand a noun with adjectives, using a comma between two.

vocabulary.definition: a describing word — it tells you more about a noun
a noun with describing words added
a tiny pause mark that sits between two adjectives

emphasize: Adjectives paint a clearer picture in the reader's head: not 'a dog' — 'a small, noisy dog'.
The rule: a COMMA between two adjectives. Two describing words? Pop a comma between them.
Build step by step: noun → one adjective → two adjectives with a comma.

keyConcepts: expanded noun phrase = noun + describing words
build up in stages: noun → one adjective → two
misconceptions: stringing two adjectives with no comma (a dark silent forest)
comma in the wrong place (after the noun, or after 'a')
using a non-adjective to expand (a run forest) — word-class slip from Lesson 16
hooks: Close your eyes: 'a dog' could be ANY dog — 'a small, noisy dog' you can really SEE.
priorKnowledge: noun = naming word, adjective = describing word (Lesson 16)

video.watchTask: Every time a noun gets described, hold up a finger per adjective — and shout 'COMMA!' when two describing words need one.

afterCheck.question: What goes between two adjectives in an expanded noun phrase?

plan.goal: Feel the difference between 'a dog' and 'a small, noisy dog' — adjectives paint the picture; retrieve the adjective test.
plan.note: The mind's-eye moment is the hook — let the child actually close their eyes and picture both.
plan.successCriteria: Child says what changed in their head between the two phrases, and names 'fluffy' as an adjective.

script.say: Close your eyes. I say: a dog. What do you picture? Could be any dog! Now I say: a small, noisy dog. Ah — now you can really SEE it! Adjectives paint a clearer picture in the reader's head. Today we'll paint pictures with words. Quick detective check first — is 'fluffy' a noun, a verb or an adjective?
script.adaptHints: Swap 'dog' for the child's pet or favourite animal. If the retrieval is shaky: 'Does it describe? A fluffy dog — yes → adjective.'

blocks.caption: a dog → a small, noisy dog — now you can SEE it!

stuckProtocol: If 'fluffy' is misnamed: recall the Lesson 16 test aloud — 'does it describe a noun? A fluffy dog — yes, adjective' — then move on.

plan.goal: Model growing a noun in three stages: castle → a dark castle → a dark, spooky castle — landing the comma rule.
plan.note: Build on the board stage by stage; the comma appears in a bold colour at stage three. Name the rule crisply each time.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees the three stages and can point to where the comma lives (between the two adjectives).

script.say: I'm going to grow a noun into a picture. Start with the noun: castle. Add ONE adjective in front: a dark castle — better! Now add a SECOND adjective — but here's the rule: put a COMMA between the two adjectives: a dark, spooky castle. The comma is a tiny pause that keeps the two describing words tidy. Noun → one adjective → two adjectives with a comma between. That whole thing — a dark, spooky castle — is called an expanded noun phrase.
script.adaptHints: Read stage three aloud with a tiny theatrical pause at the comma — 'a dark [beat] spooky castle' — so the child HEARS what the comma does.

plan.goal: Shared build: expand 'forest' from the word-bank, child places the comma; then build 'a slimy, green monster'.
plan.note: Child chooses the adjectives; the character insists on hearing where the comma goes and why.
plan.successCriteria: Child completes 'a dark, ___ forest' with an adjective and states the comma sits between the two adjectives.

script.say: Paint with me. Take 'forest'. I've started: a dark… now choose a second describing word from the bank — and where does the comma go? Fill the gap, then let's build a monster one together: a slimy, green monster!
script.adaptHints: Accept any sensible adjective aloud even if the block wants 'silent' — praise the choice, then guide to the bank word. Let the child invent the monster's adjectives verbally after.

check.question: In 'a dark, silent forest' — where does the comma go, and why?
check.expectedAnswer: Between the two adjectives (after 'dark') — it keeps the two describing words tidy.

wrongAnswers.why: word-class slip — used a verb to describe
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does 'run' DESCRIBE the forest? Run the test: 'a run forest'… Let's pick a describing word from the bank.

wrongAnswers.why: comma placed after the noun, not between the adjectives
wrongAnswers.remedy: The comma's home is BETWEEN the two describing words. Read it aloud — where's the tiny pause? Dark… silent.

plan.goal: Key diagnostic: pick the correctly punctuated expanded noun phrase — the no-comma version is the trap.
plan.note: The missing-comma option is the lesson's central misconception. Probe 'why?' after a correct answer.
plan.successCriteria: Child picks 'a dark, spooky castle' and explains the comma sits between two adjectives.

script.say: Punctuation inspector time! Three castles — only ONE is written correctly. Which one, and how do you know?
script.adaptHints: After a correct pick, probe: 'Why does that one need the comma?' Read the wrong ones aloud flat and fast to show the missing pause.

blocks.prompt: Which expanded noun phrase is punctuated correctly?
blocks.explain: Two adjectives — dark and spooky — need a comma between them: a dark, spooky castle.

check.question: Which is correct: 'a dark spooky castle', 'a dark, spooky castle', or 'a, dark spooky castle'?
check.expectedAnswer: a dark, spooky castle — the comma goes between the two adjectives

wrongAnswers.why: missing the comma between two adjectives
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it aloud — two describing words need a tiny pause between them. Where would you pop the comma?

wrongAnswers.why: comma parked after 'a' instead of between the adjectives
wrongAnswers.remedy: The comma's job is to sit BETWEEN the two describing words. Which two words is it keeping tidy?

plan.goal: Independent painting: expand castle, monster, dog into noun phrases — two adjectives + comma each time.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Watch for: missing comma; only one adjective; non-adjectives; comma after the noun.
plan.successCriteria: Child writes at least two expanded noun phrases, each with two adjectives correctly separated by a comma.

script.say: Your paintbrush now! I'll give you plain nouns — you grow each one into a picture: two describing words, comma between. Make me really SEE your monster!
script.adaptHints: Swap the nouns for the child's interests (dragon, rocket, puppy). Encourage vivid adjective choices from the bank — the comma rule never changes.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'Let's check we have two describing words and a comma.'
Step down: give the noun + one adjective; the child adds only the second adjective + comma.
ONE hint: 'Choose two describing words, then a comma between them.'
Re-ask a smaller version: one phrase straight from the bank.
Keep it safe: 'Painting with words takes practice — let's pick two and pop a comma in.'

plan.goal: Child states how to grow a noun and the comma rule; end on a win.
plan.note: Child-led; the character listens, then gives process praise tied to what actually happened.
plan.successCriteria: Child says: add adjectives to describe the noun; put a comma between two adjectives.

script.say: Tell me how to grow a plain noun into a picture — and the comma rule. … Exactly! You painted real pictures with your adjectives — and you placed the comma between them every time. The reader can really SEE your monster!
script.adaptHints: Quote back the child's own best phrase in the praise ('a slimy, green monster — I can SEE it!').

practiceBank.skill: add one adjective to a noun

wrongAnswers.why: used a verb to describe — word-class slip
wrongAnswers.remedy: Does 'bark' describe the dog or is it something the dog DOES? Pick the describing word.

wrongAnswers.why: picked another noun
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'A cat dog'? Two naming words! We want a word that tells us WHAT THE DOG IS LIKE.

hints: Which word tells you what the dog is LIKE?
Run the test: 'a ___ dog' — does it describe?

reteach.say: One adjective first, that's the whole job here. The dog is loud, so: a NOISY dog. Describing word in front, noun after. That's stage one of growing a noun.

block.caption: a noisy dog — the adjective paints the noun

practiceBank.skill: place the comma between two adjectives

wrongAnswers.why: used a full stop mid-phrase
wrongAnswers.remedy: A full stop ENDS a sentence — we're in the middle of painting! Two adjectives need the tiny pause mark. Which one is it?

wrongAnswers.why: padding with extra words instead of the comma
wrongAnswers.remedy: We don't need extra words — just the tiny pause mark between the two describing words. Pop it in.

hints: Two adjectives need a tiny pause between them.

reteach.say: Here's the rule, small and mighty: two describing words, comma between. Small COMMA noisy. Read it with the pause: a small… noisy dog. The comma keeps the two adjectives tidy.

block.definition: a small, noisy dog — the comma sits between the two describing words

practiceBank.skill: complete an expanded noun phrase from a bank

wrongAnswers.why: picked a noun — 'a dark, tree forest'
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Tree' names a thing. We need a word that DESCRIBES the forest. Which word from the bank paints it?

wrongAnswers.why: picked an adverb form
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Quietly' tells how something is DONE. We want what the forest IS LIKE — the plain describing word. Which one?

hints: The comma is already there — it's waiting for a second describing word.
Which word tells you what the forest is LIKE?

reteach.say: The phrase is half-painted: a dark, ___ forest. The comma promises a second describing word is coming. Silent describes — a dark, silent forest. Now the reader can stand inside it!

block.explain: Two adjectives — slimy and green — take a comma between them: a slimy, green monster.

wrongAnswers.why: comma missing between two adjectives
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count the describing words: slimy… green… two! What does the rule say goes between two adjectives?

wrongAnswers.why: comma pushed next to the noun
wrongAnswers.remedy: The comma sits BETWEEN the two describing words, not beside the noun. Which two words should it separate?

hints: The comma lives between the two describing words.

reteach.say: Comma inspector's trick: find the two describing words first — slimy, green. The comma goes exactly between THEM, nowhere else. A slimy, green monster. The noun never gets a comma stuck to it.

block.prompt: Paint a picture: write an expanded noun phrase for MONSTER — two adjectives and a comma.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Any two adjectives + comma + monster, e.g. 'a huge, hairy monster'

wrongAnswers.why: comma missing between two adjectives
wrongAnswers.remedy: Two describing words need a tiny pause between them — pop a comma there: a slimy, green monster.

wrongAnswers.why: only one adjective
wrongAnswers.remedy: Great start — one describing word! An EXPANDED phrase today wants two. Add a second, and remember what goes between them.

hints: Pick TWO describing words before you write.

reteach.say: Build it in stages, like the castle: monster… a slimy monster… now the second adjective AND the comma: a slimy, green monster. Noun, one adjective, two adjectives with a comma — every time.

block.prompt: Only describing words may paint! Sort the words: which could describe a castle?

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Adjectives: spooky, huge, ancient · Not: run (verb), door (noun)

wrongAnswers.why: any castle-ish word feels like it fits
wrongAnswers.remedy: Try it: 'a door castle'? Door NAMES a thing — it's a noun. Does it tell you what the castle is LIKE?

wrongAnswers.why: word-class slip from Lesson 16
wrongAnswers.remedy: Run the test: 'a run castle'… no! Run is a doing word. Which words describe?

hints: Test each word: 'a ___ castle' — does it describe?
Naming words and doing words can't paint.

reteach.say: Your Lesson 16 detective tools work here too! Only ADJECTIVES can paint a noun. Spooky castle — yes. Huge castle — yes. Run castle — no, run is a verb. Door castle — no, door is a noun. Test before you paint.

practiceBank.skill: rebuild a jumbled expanded noun phrase in a sentence

block.prompt: Word builder! Put the words back in order to make a sentence with an expanded noun phrase.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: The dark, spooky castle stood on the hill.

wrongAnswers.why: comma-word separated from its partner — comma must follow the FIRST adjective
wrongAnswers.remedy: Look at 'dark,' — it carries the comma, so it comes FIRST of the two describing words. Which order reads right?

wrongAnswers.why: adjectives placed after the noun
wrongAnswers.remedy: In an expanded noun phrase, the describing words come BEFORE the noun they paint. Where does 'castle' belong?

hints: Find the noun phrase first: which words paint the castle?
The word carrying the comma comes first of the two adjectives.

reteach.say: Find the painting team first: dark, spooky castle — two describers, then the noun. The comma rides on the first adjective. Then the sentence around it: The dark, spooky castle stood on the hill. Phrase first, sentence after.

block.title: Rebuild it
steps: Finish the sentence: …stood on the hill.

practiceBank.skill: use an expanded noun phrase in a full sentence

block.prompt: Stretch! Write a FULL sentence that uses an expanded noun phrase (two adjectives + comma). Start with your phrase, then say what it did.
block.sample: A slimy, green monster lived in the cave.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: A full sentence containing noun phrase with two comma-separated adjectives, e.g. 'A huge, hairy spider crept up the wall.'

wrongAnswers.answer: A slimy green monster lived in the cave. (no comma)
wrongAnswers.why: comma missing between the two adjectives
wrongAnswers.remedy: The sentence is lovely — now check the painting team. Two adjectives… what belongs between them?

wrongAnswers.answer: just the phrase, no sentence (a slimy, green monster)
wrongAnswers.why: stopped at the phrase
wrongAnswers.remedy: Beautiful phrase! Now give it something to DO — a verb and an ending. What did your monster do?

hints: Build the phrase first, then add what it DID.
Check: capital letter, comma between adjectives, full stop.

reteach.say: Two steps. Step one, paint the phrase: a slimy, green monster. Step two, give it a story: …lived in the cave. Phrase plus verb plus full stop — a whole picture in one sentence.

block.title: Phrase → sentence
steps: A slimy, green monster lived in the cave. ✓

practiceBank.skill: fix a phrase with a missing comma

block.prompt: Editor's desk! A friend wrote: 'a big red fast car'. What's gone wrong, and how would you fix it? (Hint: two adjectives is plenty.)
block.sample: Too many adjectives squashed together with no commas. Pick two and add the comma: a big, red car.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Spots the missing comma(s) / adjective pile-up; fixes to two adjectives with a comma, e.g. 'a big, red car'

wrongAnswers.why: shares the no-comma misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it aloud fast: bigredfastcar! No pauses. What does the rule say goes between two describing words?

wrongAnswers.why: over-corrected — comma stuck to the noun
wrongAnswers.remedy: Better pausing! But the noun never gets a comma stuck to it. Try keeping just TWO adjectives with one comma between.

hints: Count the describing words — how many is tidy?
Two adjectives, one comma, then the noun.

reteach.say: When adjectives pile up with no commas, the reader runs out of breath: a big red fast car! Editors keep it tidy: choose the two BEST describers and pop one comma between: a big, red car. Two is plenty — pick the two that paint best.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave writing, ordering and editing items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach with the three-stage build shown, then a level-1 item (one adjective, or comma-only).
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one written phrase with a correct comma and one spot-the-error item → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'expanded noun phrases'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'Let's check we have two describing words and a comma.'
Step down: give the noun + one adjective; the child adds only the second + comma.
ONE hint: 'Choose two describing words, then a comma between them.'
Re-ask a smaller version (one phrase straight from the bank), build back.
Keep it safe: 'Painting with words takes practice — let's pick two and pop a comma in.'
adaptivity.personalization: Swap the nouns for the learner's interests (dragon, rocket, puppy, princess) — the two-adjectives-and-a-comma rule never changes. Quote their best phrase back in the praise.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable phrase build; praise the process — 'you placed the comma between your adjectives every single time.'

differentiation.support: Adjective word-bank on screen to choose from; the tutor supplies the noun + first adjective, child adds the second + comma.
differentiation.stretch: Drop the bank (generate own adjectives) and put the noun phrase into a full sentence: 'A slimy, green monster lived in the cave.'

extension: Describe a made-up monster with an expanded noun phrase of two vivid adjectives — then draw it to match the words exactly.
assessmentEvidence: Child writes at least two expanded noun phrases, each with two adjectives correctly separated by a comma, and fixes one phrase with a missing comma.
revisitLater: These noun phrases feed the end-of-year writing stretch (add an expanded noun phrase to a sentence). Re-pose one phrase build as retrieval before Lesson 18.
